items.stem: Explain pro-natalist policies, referring in detail to France's family policies and to at least one other example you have studied. [7]

Support for working parents reduces the cost of children and helps sustain fertility. A second, contrasting example should be developed in the same way.

items.stem:
The resource booklet states: "About 42% of the population is under 15 and the population is projected to grow from about 220 million to over 375 million by 2050." (source: Nigeria's youthful population).

(a) Identify one quantitative piece of evidence in the extract. (b) Use it to outline stage 2-3 of the DTM.
items.answer: (a) any figure quoted from the extract with its unit/context, e.g. "About 42% of the population is under 15 and the population is projected to grow from about 220 million to over 375 million by 2050." items.stem: Using Niger as an example, explain high fertility in a low-income country.
items.answer: Niger has a TFR of about 6.7, the highest in the world, and a median age of about 15. Low female education, early marriage, limited contraception and agricultural livelihoods sustain high fertility.
items.markingKey: Context (Niger has a TFR of about 6.7, the highest in the world, and a median age of about 15.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Low female education, early marriage, limited contraception and agricultural livelihoods sustain high fertility. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to high fertility in a low-income country.

items.stem:
Case study extract - Kerala, India: With female literacy over 90%, Kerala reached replacement-level fertility in the late 1980s without coercion.

Using the extract and your own knowledge, explain how this case illustrates the role of education and health in reducing fertility.
items.answer: Investment in girls' education and healthcare reduced infant mortality and fertility voluntarily.
items.markingKey: Investment in girls' education and healthcare reduced infant mortality and fertility voluntarily. Award [1] for each valid point linking the extract to the role of education and health in reducing fertility, up to [4]; at least one point must use detail from the extract.

items.stem: In Brazil 20% of the population is aged 0-14 and 10% is aged 65+. (a) Calculate the total, youth and old-age dependency ratios. (b) Describe the likely shape of its age-sex pyramid. (c) Explain one environmental and one economic implication of this age structure.
items.answer: (a) total 43; youth 29; old-age 14 (per 100 aged 15-64) (b) more column-shaped (stationary) pyramid (c) a large working-age share can give a demographic dividend (more workers, savings and growth), but rising consumption increases resource use and emissions; falling fertility means ageing and higher pension costs will follow

items.stem: Using the case study and your own knowledge, evaluate the view that an ageing population is a greater challenge than a youthful population.
items.answer: Both create challenges; a youthful population can bring a demographic dividend if jobs and education are provided, while ageing is harder to reverse but wealthier societies have more means to adapt.
items.markingKey: Strengths / supporting points: shrinking workforce, rising pension and healthcare costs (Japan, Italy); hard to reverse low fertility. items.stem: Discuss, from more than one environmental value system, the view that population growth is the main cause of environmental problems. [9]
items.answer: Population is a factor, but consumption and technology in high-income countries drive most global environmental impact.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The ratio of the dependent population (aged 0-14 and 65+) to the working-age population (15-64), × 100"?
items.answer: dependency ratio
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of dependency ratio.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The time in years it takes for a population to double in size at a constant growth rate, approximately 70 ÷ NIR (%)"?
items.answer: doubling time (DT)
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of doubling time (DT).

items.stem: According to Boserup, population growth leads to:
items.answer: agricultural innovation that increases food production
items.markingKey: agricultural innovation that increases food production. She cited intensification such as terracing and irrigation.

items.stem: Outline the environmental implications of an ageing population.
items.answer: Slower or negative growth may reduce total resource demand, but older people may consume more energy for heating and healthcare; smaller workforces may limit investment; rural depopulation can lead to land abandonment and rewilding (e.g. Japan, Spain).
items.markingKey: Slower or negative growth may reduce total resource demand, but older people may consume more energy for heating and healthcare; smaller workforces may limit investment; rural depopulation can lead to land abandonment and rewilding (e.g. Japan, Spain). items.stem: Distinguish between total fertility rate and crude birth rate.
items.answer: CBR is births per 1,000 of the whole population per year and is affected by age structure; TFR is the average number of children per woman over her lifetime, a direct measure of fertility.
items.markingKey: CBR is births per 1,000 of the whole population per year and is affected by age structure; TFR is the average number of children per woman over her lifetime, a direct measure of fertility. items.stem: "Malthus was proved completely right by modern famines." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Global food production has outpaced population growth since 1798; modern famines are mainly caused by conflict, poverty and political failures, though Malthusian concerns resurface in debates about planetary limits.
items.markingKey: Global food production has outpaced population growth since 1798; modern famines are mainly caused by conflict, poverty and political failures, though Malthusian concerns resurface in debates about planetary limits. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Compare stage 2 of the DTM with stage 4 of the DTM.
items.answer: Stage 2 has high birth rates and rapidly falling death rates, giving rapid growth and a youthful, wide-based pyramid; stage 4 has low birth and death rates, slow growth and a more column-shaped pyramid.
items.markingKey: Stage 2 has high birth rates and rapidly falling death rates, giving rapid growth and a youthful, wide-based pyramid; stage 4 has low birth and death rates, slow growth and a more column-shaped pyramid. [1] per valid, explicit comparison up to [3].

items.stem: "Doubling time stays the same as a population grows." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Doubling time changes as the growth rate changes; most countries' growth rates are falling, so doubling times are increasing.
items.markingKey: Doubling time changes as the growth rate changes; most countries' growth rates are falling, so doubling times are increasing. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline how education of women reduces fertility.
items.answer: Educated women marry later, have greater knowledge of and access to contraception, have more employment opportunities (raising the opportunity cost of children), have healthier children (lower infant mortality) and more decision-making power.

items.stem: Outline why the world population growth rate has been falling since the late 1960s.
items.answer: Falling fertility across Asia and Latin America through education, contraception, urbanisation and policies; growth peaked at about 2.1% a year in 1968 and was below 1% by 2020.

items.stem: Describe how the shape of an age-sex pyramid changes as a country moves from stage 2 to stage 4 of the DTM.
items.answer: From a wide base and narrow top (triangular) to a narrower base, straighter sides and wider top (column/beehive) as birth rates fall and life expectancy rises.
